newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP reviewing Magma buy due diligence.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP reviewing Magma buy due diligence.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd Managing Director John Prescott said on Wednesday BHP was reviewing the due diligence process carried out when it bought U.S. copper producer Magma Copper in January for US$2.4 billion.

"I don't think there's anything that's come out since (the purchase) that goes against the due diligence, but I'm having a bit of a review of that," Prescott told reporters after an address to the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce.
"I having a look at everything that we expected would be achieved and what's been achieved," Prescott said
Prescott said he could not be specific about when Magma Copper would return to quarterly profits, "but we're working very hard to see that it's sooner rather than later."
It made a loss in the just completed first quarter.
"Hopefully what we've seen is an abberation rather than a continuing thing," he said, adding he did not know what copper prices would do.
"They are at a very low level. I don't think they're going to go up a lot in the near term."

Prescott said Magma Copper had been a profitable public company before BHP bought it. "There's no reason that the performance that Magma was sustaining as a stand-alone can't be sustained into the future," he said.
"It's not as if there's some fundamental weakness in the Magma business. The basis is there for a strong performance for BHP," he said.
Last week BHP reported a net profit of A$287 million in the three months to August 31, compared with A$372 million a year ago, due largely to a slump in profits from its copper division.
Magma had said last year before its buyout that its cash production costs were about 68 cents per pound and its costs had since jumped to about 85 cents per pound, Prescott said.
"There's some one-offs in there that we need to address and there's no doubt that we can improve on the 85 cents," he said.
Later a BHP spokesman said the review of the Magma due diligence was not a negative review and would examine what other possibilities there were for expanding Magma.

Earlier in answering a question after his address to the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce, Prescott repeated earlier comments that BHP knew it had bought Magma at the top the market when copper prices were firm.

"We knew that we were buying a quicker entrance to a broader base in that industry. It was to some extent a high risk strategy, but we had an exposure to 40 percent of the world's traded copper concentrate market," he said.

"We felt we had to have a greater number of channels for marketing that concentrate and that we had to have a secure position in a greater number of markets and that means we have to have a greater number of production points and a broader range of skills to put it all together," he said.

Prescott said BHP was rebuilding Magma Copper from the ground up rather than rationalising assets and taking out costs to make quick gains. "It was always rebuild it from the ground up and we've already put in place a new management team," he said. "But a lot more has to be done to make it successful."
